title: Operating Systems and Computer Architecture
summary: How programs execute on hardware, how memory and CPUs are organized, and how operating systems manage processes, memory, files, and hardware access.

sources.title: Operating Systems and Computer Architecture fundamentals

relationships.rationale: Instruction execution reads and updates register state.
Caches are effective because programs exhibit temporal and spatial locality.
System calls expose controlled entry points into privileged kernel services.
The scheduler selects runnable threads associated with processes.
Per-process address spaces and page permissions help provide process isolation.
Applications normally reach file-system services through system calls.
Registers are CPU-visible execution storage, while cache is a hierarchy level that transparently holds copies of memory data.

concepts.title: Instruction Cycle
concepts.firstPrinciples: A CPU runs a program by repeatedly fetching, decoding, and executing instructions.
concepts.explanation: The program counter identifies the next instruction. The CPU fetches it, decodes the operation and operands, performs the operation, and updates control state for the next instruction.

concepts.title: CPU Registers
concepts.firstPrinciples: Registers are tiny, very fast storage locations inside the CPU for active execution state.
concepts.explanation: Registers hold operands, intermediate values, addresses, flags, and control state. They are distinct from cache and main memory because instructions access them through the CPU's register interface.

concepts.title: Memory Hierarchy
concepts.firstPrinciples: Computer memory is organized as levels that trade speed, size, and cost.
concepts.explanation: Registers and caches are faster and smaller than main memory. The hierarchy works well when programs reuse nearby data or instructions, allowing faster levels to satisfy many accesses.

concepts.title: Temporal and Spatial Locality
concepts.firstPrinciples: Programs often reuse recently accessed data and access nearby addresses.
concepts.explanation: Temporal locality means recently used data is likely to be used again. Spatial locality means addresses near a recently used address are likely to be accessed soon. Caches exploit both patterns.

concepts.title: Kernel Privilege
concepts.firstPrinciples: The kernel is the privileged OS software that controls protected resources.
concepts.explanation: The kernel mediates access to memory, CPUs, devices, and files. User programs run with fewer privileges and enter kernel services through controlled interfaces.

concepts.title: System Calls
concepts.firstPrinciples: A system call is a controlled request from a user program to an operating-system service.
concepts.explanation: Opening a file, creating a process, allocating certain resources, or communicating with a device may require a system call. It is conceptually different from an ordinary function call because it crosses the user/kernel protection boundary.

concepts.title: Processes and Threads
concepts.firstPrinciples: A process is a protected running context; a thread is an execution path within that context.
concepts.explanation: Processes provide address-space and resource boundaries. Threads within one process commonly share memory and resources while having their own execution state such as a stack and registers.

concepts.title: CPU Scheduling and Context Switching
concepts.firstPrinciples: The scheduler chooses which runnable thread runs, and a context switch changes the CPU's active execution state.
concepts.explanation: The OS saves enough state for one thread and restores another so multiple activities can share a CPU. A context switch enables multiplexing but adds overhead.

concepts.title: Virtual Memory and Paging
concepts.firstPrinciples: Virtual memory gives each process an address-space view that the OS maps to physical memory.
concepts.explanation: Pages of virtual addresses map to physical frames with protection and sharing rules. A page fault occurs when an access needs OS involvement to establish or repair a mapping; it is a recoverable event in normal operation unless the access is invalid or recovery fails.

concepts.title: File Systems
concepts.firstPrinciples: A file system organizes persistent storage into named, structured objects and operations.
concepts.explanation: The OS and file-system implementation map operations such as open, read, write, and close onto storage devices while tracking names, metadata, allocation, and durability.

questions.prompt: Trace the normal CPU path for a simple instruction. Which sequence is most accurate?

choices.text: The CPU fetches, decodes, executes, then updates control state.
choices.rationale: This captures the core instruction cycle.

choices.text: The OS schedules, the compiler links, then the CPU stores the source code.
choices.rationale: Compilation and scheduling are different layers and are not the CPU's per-instruction sequence.

choices.text: The CPU writes the result to disk before it decodes the instruction.
choices.rationale: Persistent storage is not a normal step in each instruction cycle.

choices.text: The cache translates the instruction into a system call before execution.
choices.rationale: Cache may supply instruction bytes, but it does not turn instructions into system calls.

questions.explanation: The CPU fetches the instruction identified by the program counter, decodes it, executes it using registers and/or memory, then updates execution state for the next instruction.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a CPU register from a cache?

choices.text: Registers hold active execution state; caches hold likely-to-be-reused memory data.
choices.rationale: This distinguishes their roles and interfaces.

choices.text: Registers are persistent storage; caches are the OS file system.
choices.rationale: Neither is persistent storage or a file system.

choices.text: Registers belong to the kernel; caches belong to user programs.
choices.rationale: Both are hardware resources used while programs execute.

choices.text: Registers and caches are two names for the same storage level.
choices.rationale: They differ in size, access model, and purpose.

questions.explanation: Registers are explicit CPU storage locations used directly by instructions; caches transparently hold copies of memory data closer to the CPU.

questions.prompt: A loop repeatedly reads the same small array. Why might it run faster after the first pass?

choices.text: The cache may retain recently used data and nearby elements.
choices.rationale: This uses both temporal and spatial locality.

choices.text: The OS permanently converts the array into CPU instructions.
choices.rationale: Caching data is not compilation.

choices.text: The disk becomes faster because the loop repeats.
choices.rationale: The relevant speedup is usually from the memory hierarchy, not disk acceleration.

choices.text: The CPU stops executing the loop after the first pass.
choices.rationale: The loop still executes; data access may become cheaper.

questions.explanation: Repeated reads exhibit temporal locality, and nearby array elements exhibit spatial locality. The cache may satisfy later accesses without waiting for main memory.

questions.prompt: Which component normally mediates a user program's protected access to hardware and memory?

choices.text: The operating-system kernel.
choices.rationale: The kernel owns the privileged mediation role.

choices.text: The command-line shell.
choices.rationale: A shell is a user-facing command interpreter.

choices.text: A standard library function by itself.
choices.rationale: A library may wrap a system call but does not itself grant privilege.

choices.text: The file name of the program.
choices.rationale: Names do not determine hardware privilege.

questions.explanation: The kernel runs with privilege and mediates access to protected resources. A shell launches programs and a library provides reusable code, but neither is the privileged resource manager itself.

questions.prompt: Why is opening a file conceptually different from calling an ordinary helper function in the same program?

choices.text: A file open usually requires a controlled system-call transition into kernel services.
choices.rationale: This identifies the protection-boundary crossing.

choices.text: Every ordinary helper function automatically switches to kernel mode.
choices.rationale: Most ordinary function calls remain in user space.

choices.text: The file system is implemented entirely inside the CPU cache.
choices.rationale: The file system manages persistent storage through OS and device layers.

choices.text: A system call is just a compiler optimization with no OS involvement.
choices.rationale: A system call explicitly requests an OS service.

questions.explanation: Opening a file normally requests an OS/file-system service and crosses the user/kernel boundary through a system call. An ordinary helper call stays within the program's current privilege level.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a process from a thread?

choices.text: Threads usually share a process's memory; processes provide broader isolation boundaries.
choices.rationale: This captures the important resource and sharing distinction.

choices.text: A process is a single CPU register, while a thread is a disk block.
choices.rationale: Both are OS execution abstractions.

choices.text: A process is always a source-code file and a thread is always a compiler.
choices.rationale: A program file can be launched into a process, but they are not identical.

choices.text: Threads cannot share data with one another.
choices.rationale: Threads in one process commonly share address space.

questions.explanation: A process provides a protected resource and address-space context. Threads are execution paths within a process and commonly share that process's memory while keeping separate execution state.

questions.prompt: During a context switch from thread A to thread B on one CPU, what must the OS do?

choices.text: Save A's execution state and restore B's execution state.
choices.rationale: That is the core context-switch operation.

choices.text: Compile B's source code from scratch on every switch.
choices.rationale: Scheduling switches execution state; it does not compile programs.

choices.text: Copy every file on disk into B's registers.
choices.rationale: Only relevant execution state is saved/restored.

choices.text: Make A and B execute the same instruction simultaneously on the same single CPU.
choices.rationale: A context switch multiplexes time; it is not simultaneous execution on one CPU.

questions.explanation: The OS saves enough execution state for A and restores B's saved state, allowing the CPU to resume B. This multiplexes one CPU but costs time.

questions.prompt: A process accesses a virtual page whose mapping is not currently available. What can happen next?

choices.text: A page fault transfers control to the OS to resolve or reject the access.
choices.rationale: This is the normal virtual-memory mechanism.

choices.text: The cache silently becomes the process's new address space.
choices.rationale: Cache and virtual-memory mappings are different mechanisms.

choices.text: The CPU must power off because every page fault is fatal.
choices.rationale: Many page faults are recoverable.

choices.text: The program automatically receives a physical disk address as its pointer.
choices.rationale: The OS maintains mappings; a disk address is not directly handed to the program as a normal pointer.

questions.explanation: The CPU/OS can raise a page fault so the kernel can establish or repair the mapping, perhaps loading data from storage. A page fault is not automatically a crash.

questions.prompt: What does a file system add beyond raw persistent storage?

choices.text: It provides named, structured files and manages their metadata and allocation.
choices.rationale: That is the abstraction a file system provides over storage.

choices.text: It turns persistent storage into CPU registers.
choices.rationale: Storage remains a separate, slower resource.

choices.text: It guarantees that all data stays in RAM forever.
choices.rationale: A file system manages persistence, not permanent RAM residency.

choices.text: It replaces the kernel's protection boundary.
choices.rationale: File systems operate under OS/kernel control.

questions.explanation: A file system organizes storage into named objects, directories, metadata, allocation rules, and operations such as open, read, write, and close.

questions.prompt: A developer says: 'The program has a virtual address, so that must be the exact location in the RAM chip.' What is wrong with this explanation?

choices.text: A virtual address is translated to a physical location by the memory-management machinery; it is not itself a RAM location.
choices.rationale: This preserves the distinction between the process view and physical memory.

choices.text: Virtual addresses are just another name for cache lines.
choices.rationale: Cache lines are hardware storage units, not process address-space identifiers.

choices.text: Virtual addresses always point directly to disk sectors.
choices.rationale: Virtual memory may use storage during paging, but pointers are not disk-sector addresses.

choices.text: The OS does not participate in address translation.
choices.rationale: The OS establishes page tables and protection policy, with hardware performing much of the translation.

questions.explanation: A virtual address belongs to a process's address-space view. The OS and hardware translate it through page tables to a physical frame; the mapping can change and the page may not currently be in RAM.
